failing_part: "because a deterministic fill adds no imputation uncertainty, so the intervals computed afterwards remain valid"
narrowest_regime: Only by coincidence, when the fixed fill happens to sit near the conditional mean of the censored values (Berkson-like error) and the censoring fraction is small; nothing in a half-minimum rule guarantees that.
reason: A single deterministic fill is treated by the downstream model as an observed value, so it ignores the uncertainty about the censored values; absence of imputation uncertainty is the source of too-narrow intervals, not a guarantee of validity. Helsel 2006 (verified abstract) says substitution gives poor estimates, obscures or fabricates patterns, and 'should generally be considered unacceptable in scientific research', the opposite of the cited use. In my simulations (log-normal, half of the minimum detect substituted) 95% CIs for a regression slope or a group difference had coverage from 0.05 to 0.95 depending on spread and censoring fraction (e.g. exposure censored, log-sd 2, 60% below LOD: coverage 0.05, slope bias +0.18; outcome censored, log-sd 1, 60% below LOD: coverage 0.72).

citations.cite: Helsel DR (2006) Fabricating data: how substituting values for nondetects can ruin results, and what can be done about it. Chemosphere 65:2434-2439 (abstract read via Europe PMC; it argues against substitution)
Wei R et al. (2018) Sci Rep 8:663, missing value imputation for MS metabolomics (abstract: QRILC favoured for left-censored MNAR; half-minimum is one of the compared simple fills)

bite_note: Allowing half-minimum under inference while refusing a censoring-aware route sends researchers to a fill whose intervals can badly undercover; the alternative (censored-data likelihood/Tobit, multiple imputation from a censored model, or reporting a detect/non-detect sensitivity) changes the reported CI and p-value.

narrowest_regime: Plate counts from pour-plate/spiral APC methods read against a stated countable range; TNTC means the true count exceeds the range, so it is a lower bound (right-censored). QNS/hemolyzed specimens have no valid measured value for the analyte.
reason: I read the January 2026 BAM Ch. 3 PDF: it states the suitable colony counting range was updated in March 2025 from 25-250 to 15-300 per plate, and it estimates the APC by maximum likelihood 'using the plates for which exact counts are available and the too numerous to count (TNTC) plates', i.e. TNTC enters as a censored observation (a lower bound), not a dropped value. That matches the claim's censored-not-missing reading and its 15-300 figure. Treating QNS/hemolysis as a measurement failure with no value (missing) is the standard classification; the claim does not assert the missingness is ignorable.

citations.cite: FDA BAM Chapter 3: Aerobic Plate Count, January 2026 edition (PDF fetched and text extracted: range 15-300 per plate; TNTC plates enter the Poisson ML estimate as censored)
Haas CN, Heller B (1988) Averaging of TNTC counts. Appl Environ Microbiol 54:2069-2072 (cited in the BAM chapter's reference list; not opened)

bite_note: Routing TNTC to missing drops the highest-concentration samples and biases means and regressions downward; keeping them as right-censored (Tobit/survival-style or ML) changes the estimates and intervals.

narrowest_regime: MS-based metabolomics (LC/GC-MS) where missingness concentrates in low-intensity features; the hedge 'likely' matters because some missingness in low features is still random (peak-picking/alignment failures), so the pattern is evidence of a left-censored component, not proof that all of it is.
reason: A detection limit makes a value missing because of its own magnitude, which is missing-not-at-random by definition, and a missing-rate that rises as feature abundance falls is the expected signature. Wei et al. 2018 (abstract verified) treat left-censored MNAR as a distinct type and report QRILC favoured for it versus random forest for MCAR/MAR, supporting the censoring reading and its different handling. The claim is hedged ('likely') and only routes to a non-detection fill, which the user can override.

citations.cite: Wei R et al. (2018) Missing value imputation approach for mass spectrometry-based metabolomics data. Sci Rep 8:663, doi:10.1038/s41598-017-19120-0 (abstract read via Europe PMC)
Yang J et al. (2015) metabolomics missing-value/pre-processing paper cited as 'Yang 2015' (could not locate or open)

bite_note: Chooses a censoring-aware fill (half-min/QRILC family or censored model) over generic MAR imputation such as kNN/RF for the low-abundance clusters, which changes downstream means, fold-changes and tests.

failing_part: "quintiles ... estimate its dose-response as efficiently as a restricted cubic spline and without its modeling assumptions, so they rank above the spline as the primary form"
narrowest_regime: Quintiles are defensible only as a descriptive or secondary presentation (and for a trend test across categories), or when the exposure is too coarsely measured for a smooth curve; they are not more efficient or assumption-free as the primary form.
reason: Categorizing a continuous exposure discards within-category information (loss of power and residual confounding, the point of Royston-Altman-Sauerbrei 2006, whose abstract I verified is about dichotomization but whose argument extends to coarse categories), and a quintile model is itself an assumption: a step function with constant risk within each fifth. In my simulation (normal exposure, noise sd 2, truth plateau, quadratic, linear or threshold), the quintile step function had 2.1x to 4.8x the integrated MSE of a 4-knot restricted cubic spline at n=500 and 2000, and lower power for the overall association in the harder cases (0.67 vs 0.86; 0.88 vs 0.99 at n=500). The cited paper argues the opposite of the claim's direction.

citations.cite: Royston P, Altman DG, Sauerbrei W (2006) Dichotomizing continuous predictors in multiple regression: a bad idea. Stat Med 25:127-141 (abstract verified via Europe PMC: considerable loss of power and residual confounding)

bite_note: Ranking quintiles above the spline as the primary functional form changes the main model a nutrition researcher reports, trading a smooth, more precise curve for a coarse step curve with wider uncertainty and weaker detection of non-linearity.

failing_part: "not grouping by it ... is the conservative path: the held-out draw and the folds group only by a settled cluster reading"
narrowest_regime: Not grouping is the safe default only when the model will be applied to the same units it was trained on (within-unit prediction), or when the repeating column is not a unit at all (a code or category whose rows are exchangeable). For prediction to new units it is the optimistic path.
reason: With a repeating unit identifier, a random row split puts the same unit's rows on both sides, so the held-out score partly measures recognition of seen units and overstates accuracy for new units; grouping is the conservative choice for performance claims. In a simulation (100 subjects x 10 rows, subject-level covariates plus an unobserved subject effect, random forest), ungrouped 5-fold CV gave R2 = 0.62 while grouped CV gave -0.004 and the true R2 on brand-new subjects was 0.031 (8 replicates). Leaving it ungrouped until confirmed is conservative only in the sense of imposing no structure, which is the wrong sense for a held-out estimate the researcher will rely on.

citations.cite: Saeb S, Lonini L, Jayaraman A, Mohr DC, Kording KP (2017) The need to approximate the use-case in clinical machine learning. GigaScience 6:1-9 (Europe PMC summary: record-wise CV often massively overestimates accuracy; subject-wise reflects the clinical use case)

bite_note: Whether the sealed held-out set and resampling folds keep a unit's rows together decides whether the reported predictive accuracy is honest for new units or inflated (here 0.62 vs about 0.03), and which model or tuning wins in selection.

failing_part: "1.0 below 2,000 (under least squares' and the screened elastic net's 1.5)" and, more generally, the numeric ladder 2.0/1.0/3.0/2.0 whose stated basis is that it keeps "the two families the reference journeys pick today ... first"
narrowest_regime: The qualitative parts hold: ridge is a poor primary choice for inference (biased, no standard intervals), p >= n favours a shrinkage method over least squares, and tuning a penalty by inner CV from fewer than ~50 rows is noisy. The specific scores and the n=2,000 switch have no methods derivation.
reason: The only basis offered for the below-2,000 value is outcome-fitting to existing journeys, not a methods argument. The direction also looks backwards: ridge's gain over least squares comes from shrinking variance, which is largest when n is small relative to p, and shrinks as n grows. In my simulation (dense signal, correlated predictors, true R2 about 1/3, RidgeCV by efficient LOO) ridge test MSE was 0.54x OLS at n=100,p=50, 0.89x at n=500,p=100, 0.58x at n=500,p=250 and about equal (0.99x) when p/n is small, never worse; so ranking ridge below least squares for n<2,000 is unsupported wherever p/n is not tiny. Elastic net vs ridge at p >= n depends on sparsity of the truth and was not tested.
bite_note: The shelf score decides which family is recommended first at moderate n with a moderate predictor-to-row ratio, where ridge can beat least squares by a large margin in held-out error; at small p/n the families tie and the ordering is immaterial.

narrowest_regime: Residual-method adjustment where the energy-adjusted residual r = N - (a + bE) is entered with total energy E in the model and the nutrient is correlated with energy (b != 0). If b = 0, or the effect is linear, the two models coincide.
reason: Since r = N - a - bE, a spline f(r) is a function of N - bE, so f(N - bE) + g(E) equals h(N) + k(E) for all N, E only if f is linear (the mixed derivative -b f'' must vanish); for a straight line the coefficient on r equals the coefficient on N (I confirmed 0.4996 vs 0.4996). When the truth is additive in N and E, the residual spline blurs the substitution curve across the spread of energy: a step at N=0 (true -1.48 to +1.52) came out as -0.71 to +0.68 at N=+-0.5, and a hinge at 1 was smeared; the standard spline recovered the truth. Plotting f against r + (a + b*mean E) gives the energy-adjusted scale at mean energy, so the label is apt, and the standard model (spline of N with E beside it) is the route to the substitution curve. One imprecision: the residual model must include E for the equivalence statement; the claim does not say so.

citations.cite: Willett WC, Stampfer MJ (1986) Total energy intake: implications for epidemiologic analyses. Am J Epidemiol 124:17-27 (existence confirmed through a 2023 AJE commentary abstract; contents not opened)
Tomova GD et al. (2022) Theory and performance of substitution models for estimating relative causal effects of nutrients. Int J Epidemiol (search returned nothing)

bite_note: It changes how a nonlinear nutrient curve from the residual method is labelled (energy-adjusted, not isocaloric substitution) and steers a researcher who wants the substitution curve to the standard model; with a nonlinear truth the two curves visibly differ.

narrowest_regime: Two-arm (or multi-arm) cluster-randomized trial with few clusters; the t reference is only adequate when paired with a bias-corrected sandwich variance (Kauermann-Carroll or Fay-Graubard); K-2 is the stated base case, and subtracting extra cluster-level covariates is a sensible extension rather than something the cited paper tested.
reason: I read Li & Redden (PMC copy): they state that with two arms 'the degrees of freedom can be approximated as K - 2' under an assumption of no covariates, and that the GEE Wald z test should be avoided with few clusters even with bias-corrected sandwiches. Subtracting cluster-level terms (intercept, arm, cluster-constant covariates) follows the cluster-level-analysis / containment logic that only K cluster-level quantities inform those terms; the paper does not discuss covariates, so that part is derivation, not citation. In my simulation (statsmodels GEE, K=8/12/20, icc 0.05, null effect) t on K-2 beat z but with the uncorrected sandwich still undercovered (0.91 at K=8, 0.94 at K=12), whereas with a bias-reduced sandwich it was nominal to slightly conservative (0.97); the claim states only the df rule, which is correct for it.

citations.cite: Li P, Redden DT (2015) Small sample performance of bias-corrected sandwich estimators for cluster-randomized trials with binary outcomes. Stat Med 34:281-296, doi:10.1002/sim.6344 (PMC4268228 read: K-2 df for two arms, no covariates; recommends KC/FG-corrected variance with t)

bite_note: With a handful of clusters the t critical value (about 2.45 at K=8 versus 1.96 for z) widens the interval by roughly a quarter; at 30+ clusters it hardly matters.

failing_part: "In a randomized trial the primary analysis is intention to treat" as a universal, and "which randomization protects" without the requirement of complete outcome data
narrowest_regime: Superiority trials (and the treatment-policy estimand) with outcomes observed on all randomized participants or missing-data assumptions stated; for non-inferiority/equivalence trials ITT alone is not conservative and per-protocol or both are expected, and under ICH E9(R1) the primary estimand may be a different strategy if the question is about effect under adherence.
reason: The definition itself is right: White et al. (read in PMC) state that ITT 'requires all participants ... to be included in the analysis in the groups to which they were randomised, regardless of any departures from randomised treatment', and it estimates the effect of assignment. But the paper's own point is that with incomplete outcomes ITT analysis rests on untestable assumptions, so randomization protects the comparison only for the part of the outcome data that is observed or missing at random; and 'the primary analysis is ITT' is a default for superiority trials, not a rule for every randomized trial. CONSORT item 16 only asks that the report say whether the analysis was by original assigned groups, so it does not by itself establish ITT as primary.

citations.cite: White IR, Horton NJ, Carpenter J, Pocock SJ (2011) Strategy for intention to treat analysis in randomised trials with missing outcome data. BMJ 342:d40 (PMC3230114 read)
Moher D et al. (2010) CONSORT 2010 statement, item 16 (numbers analysed, 'whether the analysis was by original assigned groups'); article not opened, wording from memory
ICH E9 and E9(R1) (non-inferiority and estimand framework) from memory

bite_note: Recommending 'itt' as the trial analysis set decides whether non-adherers are analysed as assigned; in a non-inferiority trial or one with substantial post-randomization dropout the unqualified recommendation could understate the need for a per-protocol or missing-data sensitivity analysis.

failing_part: "It is refused under prediction because the model is applied to everyone" (stated as a fact about the deployment), and, more loosely, that restriction on the exposure changes the estimand to 'the effect among consumers'
narrowest_regime: Under inference, restricting to consumers narrows the target to positive intakes and must be reported; under prediction the restriction is wrong only when the model will also score non-consumers. If the intended use is among consumers (the deployment population has exposure > 0), a consumers-only training set matches the use case and refusing it is not warranted.
reason: Selecting on the exposure value is selection on a predictor, so it does not by itself bias the dose-response over x > 0 if the model is right; what is lost is the zero point and the consumer vs non-consumer contrast, so 'estimand change' is correct as a statement about the target population and extrapolation, and recording it matches STROBE-nut nut-14 (verified in PMC4896435: 'Specify if food consumption of total population or consumers only were used'), which is a reporting item, not a refusal rule. The prediction refusal is justified only by an assumption that the model will be applied to non-consumers, which the app cannot know without asking the deployment population.

citations.cite: Lachat C et al. (2016) STROBE-nut, PLoS Med 13:e1002036 (PMC4896435): nut-14 'Specify if food consumption of total population or consumers only were used to obtain results'; nut-11 on handling nonconsumers

bite_note: A researcher building a consumers-only predictor for use among consumers would be blocked by the refusal, and an inference user is told to record the change in target population rather than silently dropping zeros.

failing_part: "implies the covariates were measured at baseline, before the outcome"
narrowest_regime: As a default guess for one-row-per-person data from a cohort or trial where covariates are collected at enrolment and the outcome later; it is a probabilistic reading of the outcome's name that the user must confirm, not an implication.
reason: An outcome's name says when the outcome was measured, not when the covariates were. Counterexamples are common: a time-to-event table with covariates taken at diagnosis or at the end of follow-up, a '12m' or 'final' outcome with covariates (adherence, current intake, concurrent labs) measured at 12 months or the end, a 'change' score with mean on-study exposure, and time-varying covariates in event-time data. The author's own basis says the name only leads a guess the user confirms and cites no methods source, so 'implies' overstates it. The distinction the guess feeds is sound, though: a baseline measure of the outcome is a legitimate pre-outcome covariate (ANCOVA-type adjustment) whereas a same-time measure is a proxy of the outcome, and the with-and-without pair is a reasonable hedge. The remark that occasion labels (v1, t0, w2) do not determine timing is correct.
bite_note: Switches whether a second measure of the outcome is left out or run with-and-without, which can change the adjusted effect noticeably (baseline adjustment vs not); mitigated because the user confirms the guess.

narrowest_regime: Plausibility screens of the usual form (fixed absolute energy bounds or ratio-to-requirement cutoffs) applied to a population where most people are within the plausible range; populations that are truly extreme (very-low-energy-diet trials, inpatient or anorexia cohorts) can exceed half, which is why the refusal asks for a unit statement rather than forbidding removal outright.
reason: Published plausibility screens (e.g. Willett-type bounds of roughly 500-3,500 kcal/day for women and 800-4,200 for men) are designed to flag a few percent of respondents; if one flags a majority, the bound itself no longer applies to the data. The three listed mechanisms all shift the whole column and so flag most rows at once: kJ read as kcal multiplies values by about 4.18, a multi-day total multiplies by the number of days, and a child's or athlete's intake sits systematically outside adult bounds, whereas it is implausible that most real respondents are mis-reporters. The 0.5 cut-off itself is a convention (a smaller fraction could also signal a unit error), but the direction and the 'ask the unit first' action are sound and cheap to override.
bite_note: Prevents silently discarding more than half of a dataset and prompts the unit question, which changes both sample size and every energy-related quantity (energy adjustment, ratios) afterwards.
